title: US and Russia Strip Human-Review Safeguards From a UN Killer-Robot Pact as the General Assembly Closes, and Moscow Backs India and Brazil for Permanent Security Council Seats
subhead: As the 81st UN General Assembly wraps up, Washington and Moscow jointly gutted the core safeguards of a proposed treaty on lethal autonomous weapons, while Lavrov used the closing session to back India and Brazil for permanent Security Council seats and reject Germany and Japan.

sections.heading: Geneva Talks Gutted: US and Russia Remove Human Review From an Autonomous Weapons Framework
sections.body:
US and Russian diplomats stripped key safeguards from a proposed UN framework on lethal autonomous weapons during closed-door negotiations in Geneva earlier this month, according to a Washington Post report cited by New Kerala. The two delegations spent nearly 15 hours revising the document on the final day of talks held under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons — the UN's most advanced attempt to write rules for weapons that can identify, select and engage targets with limited or no human intervention.

The removed provisions included a requirement that humans review military targets selected by AI before an attack, standards that autonomous systems operate in a 'predictable' and 'reliable' manner, and language requiring ethical considerations. The Post reported that the talks were held behind closed doors after UN cameras were switched off and civil society observers were asked to leave, with each delegation fielding roughly 10 legal experts — nearly twice as many as most other countries. Human Rights Watch warned the weakened text could accelerate automated warfare with less accountability for civilian harm. The US State Department, Russian Foreign Ministry and the UN did not respond to the newspaper's requests for comment.
sections.whyItMatters: A US-Russia joint deletion of human-review requirements means the two largest military powers have effectively staked out a shared position against binding human control over AI weapons. Because the framework was the furthest any UN process had come on the issue, removing the veto-style safeguards leaves the field to whatever national rules the major powers choose to write — and those are the countries with the most advanced autonomous systems.

sections.heading: UN Security Council Reform: Lavrov Backs India and Brazil, Rejects Germany and Japan
sections.body:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov told the 81st UN General Assembly that Moscow supports permanent Security Council seats for India and Brazil while opposing them for Germany and Japan, according to IANS. 'UN Security Council reform cannot involve any additional seats being allocated to Western countries, especially to Germany and Japan, who are now on the path to militarism and revanchism,' Lavrov said, adding that Moscow favours broadening representation of Asia, Africa and Latin America.

The position splits the G4 coalition — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan — which met on the sidelines of the Assembly this week and jointly called for expansion in both permanent and non-permanent categories. India's candidacy also drew an endorsement from Mauritius Foreign Minister Dhananjay Ramful. Moscow separately backed greater African representation.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia is deliberately cleaving the G4, offering seats to the two members it sees as potential partners in a multipolar order while denying them to the two it frames as Western-aligned. It converts a technical reform debate into an instrument of bloc politics, and it hardens the split at the heart of the G4 that has stalled Council enlargement for years.

sections.heading: Iran Waits for a Formal US Answer After Trump Rejects the Seven-Day Hormuz Plan
sections.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran is still awaiting a formal US response to its seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, telling IRNA that any progress is conditional on its terms being met, according to Anadolu Agency. President Trump publicly rejected the plan, calling it inadequate: 'They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly,' he said, per The Hindu. Al Jazeera reported that Araghchi deliberately set aside Trump's public remarks and is waiting on mediators' response instead. Iran's armed forces separately warned Washington against intervening in the strait, saying the US would be 'slapped,' Iran International reported.

The proposal is effectively a restatement of the collapsed June memorandum of understanding, the Indian Express noted, so Trump's rejection returns both sides to their starting positions. The UN General Assembly's high-level week closed with no breakthrough in the US-Iran war.
sections.whyItMatters: Both governments are now bargaining through public statements and mediators rather than a working channel, and Tehran's decision to wait for a formal reply rather than react to Trump's remarks keeps a thread of diplomacy alive. But with the proposal merely re-treading terms the US already rejected in June, there is no new substance on the table — the war stays open with the Strait shut.

sections.heading: Ukraine: Lavrov Blames Europe for Blocking Talks as Germany Breaks Four Years of Silence
sections.body:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov accused Europe of obstructing peace efforts in his UN General Assembly address, saying 'Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the Trump administration is interested,' AFP reported via the Manila Times. Strikes over the previous 24 hours killed at least 16 people across both countries. In a notable shift, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul held a surprise 20-minute meeting with Lavrov in New York — the first direct ministerial-level contact between Berlin and Moscow since Russia's February 2022 invasion, according to Meyka. Wadephul raised Ukrainian and Russian grain exports, condemned the drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport that Germany blames on Moscow, and reaffirmed support for Ukraine's defence. Lavrov dismissed the meeting as performative, saying Berlin could have simply read its own public statements and that Germany had requested the encounter at the last minute.

On the ground, Reuters reported via the Times of India that Russian strikes shut down ArcelorMittal's electric steel plant in Ukraine — the country's biggest steelmaker — and killed seven people. An AFP analysis cited by the Hindustan Times found a surge in Russian strikes on Kyiv's warehouse infrastructure.
sections.whyItMatters: Germany's outreach signals it fears being sidelined as Trump reshapes the diplomatic map — a break from the long-standing principle of not discussing Ukraine without Ukraine. But Lavrov's rejection of the gesture, combined with continued strikes on industrial targets, shows Moscow sees little reason to negotiate while its battlefield pressure is working.

sections.heading: Saudi Crude Exports Hit a War-High as Washington Weighs a Diesel Export Ban
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia's crude exports have surged to roughly 6 million barrels per day in September — the highest since the US-Iran war began about seven months ago — despite escalating fighting, according to trade-intelligence firm Kpler via CNBC and reported by SEE News. September shipments rose nearly 80% from August's 3.4 million bpd average. The jump followed the shutdown of the East-West pipeline after a drone attack launched from Iraq, which forced the kingdom to reroute crude through the Strait of Hormuz after the US military secured a shipping corridor along the Omani coast. The seven-day average of oil exports through Hormuz stood at 13.2 million bpd on Wednesday, versus about 17 million bpd before the war.

Separately, Reuters reported via the Financial Express that Washington's talk of a possible ban on diesel exports is widening US crude futures' discount to the global benchmark.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia is exporting at a war-time high even as its own infrastructure is under attack — evidence that Gulf producers are regaining confidence in the Hormuz corridor. That is bullish for global supply and helps explain why Brent pulled back after spiking near $110 when the pipeline was hit. A US diesel export ban would be a fresh intervention in energy markets and another sign that war-driven fuel economics are now a domestic political problem in Washington.

sections.heading: Post-Summit Asia: Trump Says Xi 'Understands' His Taiwan Position as Japan Gets Briefed
sections.body: Following the US-China summit, President Trump said Chinese leader Xi Jinping 'understands' his position on Taiwan, the Japan Times reported. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Trump gave her a 'detailed' briefing on the summit in a phone call, and that Japan and the US agreed to collaborate on issues concerning China, describing the two countries as 'allies with the highest mutual trust,' according to the Straits Times. Reuters, via Devdiscourse, reported that the two powers agreed to an AI dialogue and tariff cuts on $30 billion of goods in each direction — the clearest economic breakthrough of the visit.
sections.whyItMatters: Trump's claim that Xi 'understands' his Taiwan stance is deliberately ambiguous and leaves the substance of any understanding undisclosed. Tokyo's rapid read-out signals Japan is working to make sure it is not traded away in a US-China bargain, while the $30 billion tariff cut is the concrete deliverable that will shape both economies' near-term trade.

bottomLine: The 81st UN General Assembly closed with the multilateral system's biggest players acting around it rather than through it: the US and Russia jointly stripped human-review safeguards from the UN's autonomous-weapons framework in Geneva, and Lavrov used the closing session to split the G4 by endorsing India and Brazil for permanent Council seats while rejecting Germany and Japan. On the two live wars, there was motion without progress — Washington and Tehran are trading positions through mediators over Hormuz with no new substance, and Germany broke a four-year silence with Moscow only to be told its outreach was empty. The one clear economic signal was Saudi crude exports hitting a war-high near 6 million bpd, showing Gulf supply is adapting faster than the conflict's headlines suggest.
